title: Digital Literacy for Muslims
description:
A comprehensive course designed to help Muslims navigate the digital world with confidence and Islamic consciousness. From understanding internet basics to practicing proper technology etiquette, this course bridges modern digital skills with timeless Islamic principles. Learn how to use technology as a tool for beneficial knowledge while avoiding harmful content and behaviors.

This course covers essential digital skills including email communication, online safety practices, understanding your digital footprint, and practicing proper technology etiquette. Each module connects practical digital literacy with Islamic teachings about seeking beneficial knowledge, protecting oneself from harm, and maintaining good character in all interactions.

Whether you are new to technology or looking to strengthen your digital skills with an Islamic framework, this course provides the foundational knowledge needed to engage with the digital world responsibly and purposefully.
short_description: Essential digital skills combined with Islamic principles for responsible technology use

modules.title: Introduction to the Digital World
modules.description: Understanding the basics of internet and technology with an Islamic perspective

lessons.title: What is the Internet?
lessons.content:
The internet is a global network of interconnected computers that allows people to share information, communicate, and access services from anywhere in the world. Understanding how it works helps us use it responsibly.

The Quran encourages seeking beneficial knowledge wherever it may be found. Allah says: 'So do not yield to the disbelievers, and strive against them with it [the Quran] a great striving.' (Quran 25:52) This verse reminds us that knowledge and tools can be used for noble purposes.

When we understand the basic infrastructure of the internet, we can better appreciate both its benefits and potential risks. The internet is a tool, and like any tool, its value depends on how we choose to use it. The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) taught us to seek knowledge from the cradle to the grave, and the internet provides unprecedented access to educational resources.

Key concepts include: how data travels across networks, the role of internet service providers, the difference between public and private networks, and how websites and applications function. Understanding these basics empowers us to make informed decisions about our online activities.

lessons.title: Types of Internet Connections
lessons.content:
Different types of internet connections serve different needs and purposes. Understanding these helps us choose the right service and troubleshoot problems.

Common connection types include broadband (cable or DSL), fiber optic, mobile data (3G, 4G, 5G), and satellite internet. Each has advantages and limitations in terms of speed, reliability, and cost.

The Islamic principle of moderation (wasatiyyah) applies to technology use as well. Allah says: 'And thus We have made you a justly balanced community.' (Quran 2:143) We should choose internet services that meet our needs without excess.

Factors to consider when choosing an internet connection include: the number of users in your household, the types of activities you engage in (streaming, video calls, basic browsing), your location, and your budget. Being informed consumers helps us make wise choices with our resources.

lessons.title: Web Browsers and Search Engines
lessons.content:
Web browsers (such as Chrome, Firefox, Safari, and Edge) are applications that allow you to access and view websites. Search engines (like Google, DuckDuckGo, and Bing) help you find information on the internet.

The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'Seeking knowledge is an obligation upon every Muslim.' (Sunan Ibn Majah) In our digital age, learning to effectively search for and evaluate information is an essential skill for fulfilling this obligation.

Understanding how search engines work helps you find reliable information more efficiently. Search engines use algorithms to index and rank web pages based on relevance, quality, and other factors. Learning basic search techniques, such as using quotation marks for exact phrases and minus signs to exclude terms, can significantly improve your search results.

It is important to develop critical thinking skills when evaluating online information. Not all sources are equally reliable, and learning to assess the credibility of websites and authors is a crucial digital literacy skill. The Islamic tradition emphasizes the importance of verifying information before acting upon it.

modules.title: Email Communication
modules.description: Mastering professional and personal email communication

lessons.title: Setting Up an Email Account
lessons.content:
Email remains one of the most important forms of digital communication. Setting up an email account is often the first step in establishing your digital identity.

Major email providers include Gmail (Google), Outlook (Microsoft), and Yahoo Mail. When choosing an email provider, consider factors such as storage space, security features, ease of use, and privacy policies.

The Islamic principle of trust (amanah) applies to email communication. When you create an email account, you are entrusting the provider with your personal information. Choose providers that demonstrate respect for user privacy and data protection.

Steps to set up an email account typically include: choosing a username that represents you appropriately, creating a strong password, setting up recovery options, and configuring your profile information. Your email address often serves as your primary digital identifier for various online services.

lessons.title: Writing Professional Emails
lessons.content:
Good email communication reflects your character and professionalism. The way we communicate online should reflect the Islamic values of respect, honesty, and clarity.

The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him speak good or remain silent.' (Sahih al-Bukhari) This hadith applies to all forms of communication, including email.

Key elements of professional emails include: a clear and descriptive subject line, appropriate greeting and closing, concise and well-organized content, proper grammar and spelling, and a professional tone. Avoid using all caps, excessive punctuation, or informal language in professional correspondence.

When composing emails, consider your audience and purpose. Business emails should be formal and direct, while personal emails can be more casual. Always proofread before sending, and be mindful of who can see your email through the To, Cc, and Bcc fields.

lessons.title: Email Safety and Etiquette
lessons.content:
Email safety is essential for protecting yourself and others from various online threats. Being cautious with email helps prevent phishing attacks, malware infections, and privacy breaches.

The Quran advises: 'O you who believe, be persistently standing firm in justice, witnesses for Allah, even if it be against yourselves or parents and relatives.' (Quran 4:135) This principle of vigilance and responsibility extends to our digital interactions.

Never open attachments or click links from unknown senders. Be suspicious of emails that create urgency, request personal information, or contain grammatical errors. These are common signs of phishing attempts. When in doubt, verify the sender through another communication channel.

Email etiquette includes: responding to emails in a timely manner, using Reply All appropriately, being mindful of email length, respecting others' time, and maintaining confidentiality. Forwarding emails without permission and sending chain letters are considered poor etiquette and may violate privacy.

modules.title: Online Safety and Digital Footprint
modules.description: Protecting yourself and understanding your online presence

lessons.title: Understanding Your Digital Footprint
lessons.content:
Your digital footprint is the trail of data you leave behind when using the internet. This includes websites visited, emails sent, social media posts, online purchases, and any other online activity.

There are two types of digital footprints: active (what you intentionally share) and passive (data collected without your direct knowledge). Understanding both helps you manage your online presence.

The Islamic concept of accountability (hisab) reminds us that we will be accountable for our actions. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'The feet of a servant will not move on the Day of Judgment until he is asked about his life and how he spent it, his knowledge and what he did with it, his wealth and how he earned and spent it, and his body and how he used it.' (Sunan al-Tirmidhi)

Your digital footprint can affect college admissions, job opportunities, and personal relationships. Being mindful of what you share online is an important aspect of maintaining your reputation and protecting your privacy.

lessons.title: Protecting Your Personal Information
lessons.content:
Protecting personal information online is essential for your safety and security. Personal information includes your full name, address, phone number, date of birth, financial information, and identification numbers.

The Quran emphasizes the importance of protection: 'Indeed, Allah is ever, over you, a Guardian and a Protector.' (Quran 4:45) While we trust in Allah's protection, we are also commanded to take practical measures to safeguard ourselves.

Never share sensitive personal information on public forums, social media, or with unknown parties. Be cautious about what information you provide when signing up for online services. Read privacy policies to understand how your data will be used and shared.

Use strong, unique passwords for different accounts, enable two-factor authentication when available, and regularly review your account settings. Being proactive about security helps prevent identity theft and other forms of cybercrime.

lessons.title: Recognizing Online Threats
lessons.content:
Being able to identify common online threats helps you protect yourself and your family. These threats include phishing scams, malware, identity theft, cyberbullying, and inappropriate content.

The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'Part of the perfection of a person's Islam is his leaving that which does not concern him.' (Sunan al-Tirmidhi) This wisdom applies to avoiding unnecessary risks and questionable content online.

Phishing is a technique used by scammers to trick you into revealing personal information. Malware includes viruses, spyware, and other malicious software. Identity theft occurs when someone uses your personal information without permission. Cyberbullying involves harassment or threats through digital communication.

Learn to recognize warning signs: unexpected emails or messages, requests for personal information, too-good-to-be-true offers, pressure to act quickly, and unusual account activity. When you encounter these signs, stop, think, and verify before taking action.

modules.title: Technology Etiquette and Islamic Values
modules.description: Applying Islamic principles to modern technology use

lessons.title: Adab (Etiquette) of Digital Communication
lessons.content:
Islamic adab (etiquette) encompasses all aspects of life, including how we use technology. The principles of respect, honesty, kindness, and moderation should guide all our digital interactions.

Allah says in the Quran: 'And speak to people good [words].' (Quran 2:83) This command applies equally to our face-to-face conversations and our digital communications. The words we type carry the same weight as words spoken aloud.

When communicating online, remember that there is a real person on the other end. Avoid being harsh, dismissive, or disrespectful, even in disagreements. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him speak good or remain silent.' (Sahih al-Bukhari)

Practice digital adab by: thinking before you post, avoiding gossip and backbiting online, being patient with others, correcting mistakes privately when possible, and maintaining humility. Remember that your online behavior reflects your character and your faith.

lessons.title: Balancing Screen Time and Life
lessons.content:
Maintaining a healthy balance between technology use and other aspects of life is essential for physical, mental, and spiritual well-being. Excessive screen time can affect sleep, relationships, productivity, and worship.

The Islamic principle of wasatiyyah (moderation) guides us in all matters. Allah says: 'And do not make your hand [as] chained to your neck or extend it completely and [thereby] become blamed and insolvent.' (Quran 17:29) This verse teaches moderation in spending, which applies to how we spend our time as well.

Set intentional limits on recreational screen time. Designate specific times for checking social media and emails. Create technology-free zones in your home, especially during meals and before sleep. Use screen time tracking tools to monitor your usage patterns.

Make time for activities that nourish your soul: Quran recitation, dhikr (remembrance of Allah), prayer, exercise, family time, and community involvement. Technology should enhance your life, not dominate it.

lessons.title: Using Technology for Good
lessons.content:
Technology can be a powerful tool for spreading beneficial knowledge, connecting with the Muslim community, and performing acts of worship. The key is to use technology with intention and purpose.

The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'Convey from me, even if it is one verse.' (Sahih al-Bukhari) In the digital age, sharing beneficial content online is a form of conveying the message of Islam.

Useful applications of technology for Muslims include: accessing Quran and hadith apps, joining online Islamic classes, participating in virtual community events, supporting charitable causes through online platforms, and using productivity tools to manage time and responsibilities.

Remember that technology is a means, not an end. The goal is to use these tools to become better Muslims, strengthen our relationship with Allah, and benefit humanity. As Allah says: 'You are the best community raised for mankind. You enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong and believe in Allah.' (Quran 3:110)
